en.html:
I will say it plainly: I have never found it pleasant, this tearing up through the sky toward the zenith. It only ever made my skin rise in goose-bumps of fear. A bottomless pit, an end past the end, the realm of nothing—the unknown. Knowing I was driving myself straight into it, I felt a cold awe sting down my spine.

Gattari's thrust was a little lower than usual. The altitude was not climbing the way I expected. Today the <ruby>sky itself was sluggish<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>.

Evidently we were short of caloric energy. Even so, no ordinary opponent should get the better of us...

A cheerful <ruby>armor communication<rt>metal-echo</rt></ruby> struck my ears. Whatever the words admitted, there was not a trace of regret in his voice.

Hasso: the sword held at one's <ruby>side<rt>side</rt></ruby>, parallel to the body. A thrust from that guard is not mainstream in warrior combat, because spearing a warrior who comes flying at speed is far harder than cutting him down.

But if that difficulty is overcome and the point finds the enemy, a warrior's diamond force gathered into one single point will go through even plate that laughs at cannon shells, as if it were thin paper!

Probably no warrior alive can survive a perfect thrust. For that reason the technique is generally kept for one situation: the last-ditch comeback from a losing position.

I lowered the horn and raised speed. The wind <ruby>went hard<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>.

The enemy was a speed-centered single-pointed armor. Whether I could shake him off was difficult to say, but there was nothing to do except try.

Chasing from behind, it would be hard to land a fatal blow. A warrior's plate is extremely tough; it can only be cut through with the impact of a head-on collision.

Besides, nearing the ground made any attack more dangerous. A pursuer diving at the fleeing target from above could easily strike the ground instead.

I had to be ready to take a blow or two. But if I did not panic and err, we would not suffer excessive damage. Or so it should be—
